messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 49

She is nineteen and grew up on a small island where work begins before sunrise and the sea shapes nearly every part of daily life. Fishing is not just her job; it is the rhythm of her family, the way money comes in, the way mornings smell, the way people measure whether a day has been good or bad. She has been going out on boats since she was a child, first with older relatives and later as one of the youngest people on the crew in her own right. She speaks about the ocean with affection and caution, as if it is both a provider and something that never promises mercy.

The event she returns to again and again happened a little over a year ago. She was on a small fishing boat with two older men from her community, one of whom had known her since she was a child. The weather had seemed manageable when they left. She remembers the ordinary details with painful clarity: the wet coils of rope under her feet, the diesel smell, one of the men joking that she worked harder than most boys her age. By midday the water had changed. Wind picked up quickly, and what had felt routine became confused and urgent. She remembers being told to hold fast, to keep low, to grab the net line. Then one of the men was thrown off balance as the boat lurched. She sees it over and over: his body hitting the side, his arm reaching, the sudden splash, the stunned silence before anyone shouted.

They tried to pull him back, but the sea was rough and the boat kept swinging away from him. She can still hear his voice calling once, then not again. She remembers staring at the patch of water where his head had been, as if looking hard enough could bring him back. She froze when the others moved. Later she tells the story with shame, saying her hands stopped working, her mind went blank, and she became "useless" while the others searched. They never found him.

In the days afterward, the whole island seemed to know before she was ready to speak. There were prayers, visitors, food brought to the family, and quiet looks toward her, not blaming exactly, but searching her face for the story. She attended the mourning rituals and stood near his relatives feeling as if she did not deserve to be there. At night she lay awake hearing water strike the boat again and again. When she did sleep, she woke suddenly with her heart racing, certain she had heard someone shouting her name from outside.

At first she told herself she just needed time. Instead, the world grew smaller. She still worked because work was expected and because fishing was how she contributed at home, but getting onto a boat became a private ordeal. Before dawn she often feels sick, tying and retying knots, checking equipment repeatedly, scanning the horizon for signs of changing weather long before anyone else is worried. If someone moves too quickly near the edge, her whole body stiffens. She startles at splashes. When the boat rocks unexpectedly, she feels herself leave the present for a second and she is back in that moment, watching a man disappear.

She avoids talking about him with others from the crew, and she avoids the part of shore where they returned that day. Her boyfriend notices before she says anything directly. He tells her she is somewhere else even when she is sitting right beside him. She used to laugh easily with him and stay out with cousins in the evening. Now she often wants to go home early, especially if people are drinking and retelling stories from the sea. Sometimes when he reaches for her unexpectedly, she flinches and then feels guilty. She worries he sees her as changed, less warm, less alive.

She carries a heavy belief that she failed. Intellectually, she knows the sea was dangerous and the men around her struggled too, but in quieter moments her thoughts turn harsh and repetitive: she should have moved faster, shouted louder, done something different. These thoughts come uninvited while she is cleaning fish, mending nets, or trying to eat with her family. She has become more irritable and then ashamed of that too. Small frustrations make her snap at people she loves. Afterward she withdraws, sitting alone outside the house where she can hear the surf but not see it.

What troubles her most is that the ocean still calls to her. She does not want to leave fishing; it is part of who she is, part of where she belongs. Yet every trip asks her to step back into the place where she learned, in the most intimate way, how quickly a life can vanish. She keeps going out, keeps working, keeps her eyes on the lines and the weather and the men around her, but she no longer trusts the day to remain ordinary. Some part of her is always bracing for the next shout, the next splash, the next moment when everything changes.
